metadata.title: Bagging Predictors
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF->text fallback; .tex source not available. Math fidelity reduced.

nodes.name: Learning set
nodes.statement: A learning set $\mathcal{L}$ consists of data $\{(y_n, x_n), n=1,\ldots,N\}$ where the $y_n$ are either class labels or a numerical response, used to form a predictor $\varphi(x; \mathcal{L})$.
nodes.statement_clean: A learning set is a finite sample of input-output pairs used to fit a predictor.

nodes.name: Aggregated predictor (numerical)
nodes.statement: Given replicate learning sets $\{\mathcal{L}_k\}$, the aggregated predictor for a numerical response is $\varphi_A(x) = E_\mathcal{L}\, \varphi(x; \mathcal{L})$, the expectation of the predictor over the learning-set distribution.
nodes.statement_clean: For numerical y, the aggregated predictor averages the predictor across learning sets.

nodes.name: Aggregated predictor (classification, voting)
nodes.statement: If $\varphi(x; \mathcal{L})$ predicts a class $j \in \{1,\ldots,J\}$, the aggregated predictor by voting is $\varphi_A(x) = \arg\max_j N_j$ where $N_j = \#\{k : \varphi(x;\mathcal{L}_k) = j\}$.
nodes.statement_clean: For class labels, the aggregated predictor is the plurality vote across learning sets.

nodes.name: Bootstrap replicate learning set
nodes.statement: A bootstrap replicate $\mathcal{L}^{(B)}$ of $\mathcal{L}$ consists of $N$ cases drawn at random with replacement from $\mathcal{L}$; each $(y_n,x_n)$ may appear repeated times or not at all.
nodes.statement_clean: A bootstrap replicate is an N-sample drawn with replacement from the original learning set.

nodes.name: Bagged predictor
nodes.statement: The bagged predictor is $\varphi_B(x) = \mathrm{av}_B\, \varphi(x; \mathcal{L}^{(B)})$ for numerical $y$, and the plurality vote of $\{\varphi(x; \mathcal{L}^{(B)})\}$ for class-label $y$. The acronym 'bagging' stands for bootstrap aggregating.
nodes.statement_clean: Bagging averages (or votes among) predictors fit on bootstrap replicates of the learning set.

nodes.name: Bootstrap distribution $P_\mathcal{L}$
nodes.statement: $P_\mathcal{L}$ is the empirical distribution placing mass $1/N$ at each point $(y_n,x_n) \in \mathcal{L}$; it is the bootstrap approximation to the true distribution $P$.
nodes.statement_clean: The bootstrap distribution is the empirical measure of the learning set.

nodes.name: Average prediction error (regression)
nodes.statement: For predictor $\varphi(x;\mathcal{L})$ with $(Y,X) \sim P$ independent of $\mathcal{L}$, the average squared prediction error is $e = E_\mathcal{L}\, E_{Y,X}(Y - \varphi(X;\mathcal{L}))^2$.
nodes.statement_clean: The expected squared error of a predictor averaged over learning sets and test draws.

nodes.name: Aggregated prediction error
nodes.statement: The error of the aggregated predictor $\varphi_A$ is $e_A = E_{Y,X}(Y - \varphi_A(X;P))^2$.
nodes.statement_clean: Squared error of the aggregated predictor against the true distribution.

nodes.name: Class-conditional vote distribution $Q(j|x)$
nodes.statement: $Q(j \mid x) = P_\mathcal{L}(\varphi(x;\mathcal{L}) = j)$, the probability over the learning-set distribution that the predictor assigns class $j$ at input $x$.
nodes.statement_clean: Probability that the random predictor outputs class j at x.

nodes.name: Order-correct (set $C$)
nodes.statement: $C = \{x : \arg\max_j P(j \mid x) = \arg\max_j Q(j \mid x)\}$, the set on which the aggregated predictor's modal class agrees with the Bayes optimal class.
nodes.statement_clean: The set of inputs where the voting class matches the Bayes class.

nodes.name: Bayes (optimal) classifier
nodes.statement: The highest attainable correct-classification predictor is $Q^*(x) = \arg\max_j P(j \mid x)$ with rate $r^* = \int \max_j P(j \mid x)\, P_X(dx)$.
nodes.statement_clean: The Bayes optimal classifier picks the class with maximal posterior at each x.

nodes.name: Instability of a predictor
nodes.statement: A procedure $\varphi$ is unstable if small changes in the learning set $\mathcal{L}$ can produce large changes in $\varphi(\cdot;\mathcal{L})$; otherwise it is stable. Examples: trees, neural nets, subset selection are unstable; $k$-nearest-neighbor is stable.
nodes.statement_clean: Instability means small data perturbations cause large changes in the fitted predictor.

nodes.name: Forward variable selection
nodes.statement: Given a current model on variables $x_{m_1},\ldots,x_{m_k}$, for each $m \notin \{m_1,\ldots,m_k\}$ fit the regression of $y$ on $(x_{m_1},\ldots,x_{m_k},x_m)$, compute $\mathrm{RSS}(m)$, and add $x_{m_{k+1}}$ minimizing $\mathrm{RSS}(m)$; $\varphi_k$ is the linear regression on the chosen $k$ variables.
nodes.statement_clean: A greedy variable-entry algorithm for linear regression.

nodes.name: Aggregation reduces mean-squared error
nodes.statement: Under the regression setup, $e \geq e_A$, with equality only when $\varphi(x;\mathcal{L})$ is constant in $\mathcal{L}$; the gap depends on how unequal $[E_\mathcal{L}\varphi(x;\mathcal{L})]^2$ and $E_\mathcal{L}\varphi^2(x;\mathcal{L})$ are.
nodes.statement_clean: Aggregation always lowers (or matches) the mean-squared prediction error.
assumptions: $(y,x)$ pairs in $\mathcal{L}$ are i.i.d. from distribution $P$
conclusions: $e \geq e_A$ where $e = E_\mathcal{L} E_{Y,X}(Y-\varphi(X;\mathcal{L}))^2$ and $e_A = E_{Y,X}(Y-\varphi_A(X;P))^2$
The gap is governed by the variance of $\varphi(x;\mathcal{L})$ over $\mathcal{L}$

nodes.name: Aggregation in classification: near-optimality on the order-correct set
nodes.statement: If $x \in C$ then $\sum_j I(\arg\max_i Q(i\mid x)=j) P(j\mid x) = \max_j P(j\mid x)$, so $r_A = \int_{x\in C}\max_j P(j\mid x)\,P_X(dx) + \int_{x\notin C}\sum_j I(\varphi_A(x)=j) P(j\mid x)\,P_X(dx)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Wherever voting picks the Bayes class, the aggregated classifier achieves the Bayes rate; aggregation can transform good classifiers into nearly optimal ones, but poor ones into worse ones.
conclusions: On the order-correct set $C$, $\varphi_A$ attains the Bayes correct-classification rate
If $P_X(C)\approx 1$, $\varphi_A$ is nearly optimal even when $\varphi$ is far from optimal
If $\varphi$ is poor (low $Q$ on the right class), aggregation can degrade performance

nodes.name: Bagging helps unstable, hurts stable procedures
nodes.statement: Bagging $\varphi_B = \varphi_A(x;P_\mathcal{L})$ is caught between two effects: instability allows aggregation to improve accuracy, while stability makes $\varphi_A(x;P_\mathcal{L})$ less accurate than $\varphi(x;\mathcal{L})$ for data drawn from $P$.
nodes.statement_clean: Bagging is beneficial for unstable predictors and can hurt stable ones; there is a cross-over point.

nodes.name: Bagging classification trees
nodes.statement: Procedure that constructs 50 bootstrap classification trees (with 10-fold CV pruning) and predicts by plurality vote on a held-out test set.
input: Learning set $\mathcal{L}$ and test set $\mathcal{T}$ (random split of the data set)

nodes.name: Random train/test split
nodes.statement: Randomly divide the data set into a learning set $\mathcal{L}$ and a test set $\mathcal{T}$, with the test-set size chosen so that $\mathcal{L}$ is reasonably large.

nodes.name: Single-tree baseline
nodes.statement: Construct a classification tree from $\mathcal{L}$ with selection by 10-fold cross-validation; run the test set through it to get $e_S(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{T})$.

nodes.name: Bootstrap loop over trees
nodes.statement: For $k=1,\ldots,50$: draw bootstrap sample $\mathcal{L}_B$ from $\mathcal{L}$ and grow a tree $\varphi_k$ using $\mathcal{L}_B$ with 10-fold cross-validation.

nodes.name: Plurality vote on test set
nodes.statement: For each $(j_n,x_n)\in\mathcal{T}$, the estimated class is the plurality of $\varphi_1(x_n),\ldots,\varphi_{50}(x_n)$; the proportion of mismatches with the truth is $e_B(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{T})$.

nodes.name: Average over 100 random splits
nodes.statement: Repeat the random division 100 times and report the averaged $e_S$ and $e_B$.

nodes.name: Bagging regression trees
nodes.statement: Procedure that constructs 25 bootstrap regression trees (with 10-fold CV pruning) and predicts by averaging on a held-out test set.

nodes.name: Train/test split and baseline tree
nodes.statement: Split data into $\mathcal{L}$ and $\mathcal{T}$ (or generate $|\mathcal{L}|=200$, $|\mathcal{T}|=1000$ for simulated sets); grow a regression tree on $\mathcal{L}$ with 10-fold CV and compute $e_S(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{T})$.

nodes.name: Bootstrap loop over regression trees
nodes.statement: Generate 25 bootstrap replicates $\mathcal{L}^{(B)}$; on each, grow a regression tree $\varphi_k$ with 10-fold CV, giving predictors $\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_{25}$.

nodes.name: Average predictions and compute test error
nodes.statement: For each $(y_n,x_n)\in\mathcal{T}$, set $\hat{y}_B = \mathrm{av}_k\, \varphi_k(x_n)$; compute $e_B(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{T})$ as the test-set MSE between $\hat{y}_B$ and $y$, then average over 100 repetitions.

nodes.name: Bagging forward subset selection (linear regression)
nodes.statement: Procedure that runs forward variable selection on each of 50 bootstrap replicates and averages the $m$-variable predictors to form bagged sequences $\varphi_1^{(B)},\ldots,\varphi_M^{(B)}$.
input: Learning set $\mathcal{L}$ from the linear model $y=\sum_m \beta_m x_m + \epsilon$
Number of variables $M$ and bootstrap replicates (50)
output: Sequence of bagged predictors $\varphi_1^{(B)}(x),\ldots,\varphi_M^{(B)}(x)$ and their MSEs $e_1^{(B)},\ldots,e_M^{(B)}$
Comparison sequence $e_1^{(S)},\ldots,e_M^{(S)}$ from unbagged forward selection

nodes.name: Bagging class probability estimates
nodes.statement: For methods that estimate $\hat{p}(j\mid x)$, average the estimates over bootstrap replicates to form $\hat{p}_B(j\mid x)$, then classify by $\arg\max_j \hat{p}_B(j\mid x)$.

nodes.name: Aggregation MSE inequality (Jensen)
nodes.statement: Using $(EZ)^2 \leq EZ^2$: $e = EY^2 - 2EY\varphi_A + E_{Y,X}E_\mathcal{L}\varphi^2(X;\mathcal{L}) \geq E(Y-\varphi_A)^2 = e_A$.

nodes.name: Correct classification rate decomposition
nodes.statement: $r = \sum_j \int Q(j\mid x) P(j\mid x) P_X(dx)$; $r_A = \sum_j \int I(\arg\max_i Q(i\mid x)=j) P(j\mid x) P_X(dx)$.

nodes.name: Coefficient template (linear simulation)
nodes.statement: Each cluster of regression coefficients has the form $\beta_m = c[(h - |m-k|)_+]^2$ for $m=1,\ldots,30$, where $k$ is the cluster center and $h \in \{1,3,5\}$ controls cluster width; $c$ is normalized so $R^2 \approx 0.75$.

nodes.name: Friedman #1 model
nodes.statement: $y = 10\sin(\pi x_1 x_2) + 20(x_3 - 0.5)^2 + 10 x_4 + 5 x_5 + \epsilon$ with $\epsilon \sim N(0,1)$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_{10}$ uniform on $[0,1]$.

nodes.name: Friedman #2 model
nodes.statement: $y = (x_1^2 + (x_2 x_3 - 1/(x_2 x_4))^2)^{1/2} + \epsilon_2$ with $\epsilon_2 \sim N(0,\sigma_2)$ and ranges $0\leq x_1\leq 100$, $20\leq x_2/(2\pi)\leq 280$, $0\leq x_3\leq 1$, $1\leq x_4\leq 11$.

nodes.name: Friedman #3 model
nodes.statement: $y = \arctan\!\left(\frac{x_2 x_3 - 1/(x_2 x_4)}{x_1}\right) + \epsilon_3$ with the same predictor ranges as Friedman #2 and signal-to-noise ratio $3:1$.

nodes.name: Bagging classification trees on seven UCI/simulated data sets
nodes.statement: Bagging (50 replicates) applied to classification trees on waveform, heart, breast cancer, ionosphere, diabetes, glass, soybean reduces test misclassification by 20-47% versus a single tree (Table 1).

nodes.name: Bagging regression trees on five data sets
nodes.statement: Bagging (25 replicates) applied to regression trees on Boston Housing, Ozone, Friedman #1/2/3 reduces test mean-squared error by 22-46% versus a single tree (Table 3).

nodes.name: Linear-regression subset selection illustration
nodes.statement: Simulated $M=30$, $N=60$ linear models with three coefficient regimes ($h=1,3,5$): bagging matches or beats forward subset selection at the optimal $m$ but degrades for large $m$ where regression is stable.

nodes.name: Number of bootstrap replicates on waveform
nodes.section: 6.2 How Many Bootstrap Replicates Are Enough?
nodes.statement: On the waveform data, bagged misclassification rates with 10/25/50/100 replicates are 21.8/19.5/19.4/19.4% (vs. 29.0% unbagged), so most of the gain is captured by 10-25 replicates.

nodes.name: Bagging nearest neighbors does nothing
nodes.statement: On six data sets, bagged nearest-neighbor misclassification $e_B$ exactly equals the single-classifier rate $e_S$ (Table 5), confirming nearest neighbor's stability under bootstrap perturbation.

nodes.name: Bagged class-probability estimates on waveform
nodes.statement: On the simulated waveform data, the average error $|\hat{p}(j\mid x) - p(j\mid x)|$ over test cases drops from 0.189 (single tree) to 0.124 (bagged), a 34% decrease.

nodes.name: Bagging as embarrassingly parallel
nodes.section: 6.2 How Many Bootstrap Replicates Are Enough?
nodes.statement: Bagging is 'almost a dream procedure for parallel computing': constructing a predictor on each $\mathcal{L}^{(B)}$ requires no inter-CPU communication.

nodes.name: Why bagging leaves nearest neighbors unchanged
nodes.statement: With $N$ bootstrap draws, each training case appears with probability $\approx 1 - 1/e \approx 0.632$; for the bagged 1-NN classification of a test point to differ from the unbagged one, its nearest neighbor must be absent from at least half of $N_B$ replicates, an event whose probability decays as $N_B$ grows.

nodes.name: Trade-off: interpretability vs. accuracy
nodes.statement: What one loses with bagged trees is a simple, interpretable structure; what one gains is increased accuracy, with bagging adding only a wrapper loop around any existing procedure.
